messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Difficulty compiling Stan [and memory issues after that]
messages.body_plain:
Nick,

Thanks for attaching the simple model. Unfortunately, I can't get it to work. I can't sample B1, B2, B3, B4 properly. I didn't want to spend too much time debugging what you have. Instead, I've created a model that works.

My guess is that you really want the Dirichlet distribution instead of a multinomial -- that's from seeing the data and realizing your data are continuous. I'll write out both models, in case you have integer data. I've renamed the variables to something more general.

Multinomial (discrete data)
------------------------------------
data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  int ns[N,4];
}
parameters {
  simplex[4] B;
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    ns[n] ~ multinomial(B);
  }
}

Dirichlet (continuous data)
------------------------------------
data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  vector[4] ns[N];
}
parameters {
  simplex[4] B;
}
model {
  for (n in 1:N) {
    B ~ dirichlet(ns[n]);
  }
}

------------------------------------

First, notice the difference in data declaration. For multinomial, I've declared a 2D array of integers. For Dirichlet, it's a N-length array of 4-vectors.

Second, I've gotten rid of the transformed data block. Here, you want to declare the B's in the original model as a simplex. There's no need to try to do any trickiness -- Stan can handle it all under the hood for you.

If you wanted to try it out on more simple data first, you can replace the data block with a transformed data block like:

transformed data {
  int <lower=0> N;
  vector[4] ns[100];
  N <- 100;
  for (n in 1:100) {
    ns[n,1] <- 1;
    ns[n,2] <- 10;
    ns[n,3] <- 100;
    ns[n,4] <- 1000;
  }
}

Hopefully that helps and you can really simplify your model. If you want documentation on the distributions, you'll find them in the manual.

When we suggest breaking down your model, these are sort of the steps we take. Even with the Dirichlet example, I put in fake data (as shown), where I knew the expected parameter values. I had original swapped the parameters and the variables since I was working with the multinomial first (written as 'ns[n] ~ dirichlet(B)') and it was clearly not right. I wouldn't have been able to pick that out if I used the full dataset to begin with. I also wouldn't have been able to debug it as quickly if there were lots of things happening in transformation blocks or restrictive priors. I guess I don't have the ability to intuit parameters through a thick model.

Anyway, let us know how you get on with the rest of your model.

Daniel

On Fri, Sep 27, 2013 at 2:16 PM, Nick Menzies <nick.m...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Daniel,
>
> Sure thing -- simple model attached. It is a quick hack to make sure that the mean of the posterior conforms to the mean in the data, so forgive the unconventional prior.
>
> For the gradient tests -- sorry I didnt send those earlier, only just realized I could access these using rStan (not sure how to use the command line version, so had not moved on that yet). When I run stan with test_grad=TRUE, the gradients produced have no NaNs, though am unsure what represents good behavior. When I compare the finite difference result with the autodiff result the differences are pretty small except for some parameters right down the bottom (124-136). I am not sure how the parameters are indexed, but I assume these parameters at the bottom are the priors for the mortality rate ratios, which are gamma distributions with very strong priors. I am not sure why these would behave differently, but they are not the focus of inference, and prior should really equal posterior for these parameters. However, the inits for these parameters may be way off (given the strong prior) , so that may be something.
>

> > >
> > > So what to do?  From earlier posts on the subject of max_treedepth I see that the default is a bit arbitrary, but small values mean that the benefits of HMC are not really being harnessed (if I am interpreting Mike's comment on this <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/max_treedepth/stan-users/3-yyH1q4MGs/sZyjT-g5AKwJ> thread correctly). I can probably answer my research question with a smaller sample (10 states instead of 52), so I might have something that works, but I have a feeling (just from the earlier posts on the subject) that a max_treedepth of 5 may just be silly.

> > > > the calculations into C++.  Stan isn't really engineered for building
> > > > large code bases --- no namespace support, no stepwise debuggers, very
> > > > weak printing and exception control, etc.
> > > >
> > > > I am confused now.. is is possible to have some part of the model coded separately in C++ with the results passed back to Stan?  I assume not, but thought I should check.  If everything is running as intended, I see my possible problems as:
> > > > 1. Large parameter space: if I ever get the full model working it will have ~250 parameters, which is a lot, however other users seem to have successfully dealt with problems with many more parameters, so I am assuming this okay for now.
> > > > 2. Lots of data: in the full model I would be evaluating 4.9 x10^5 likelihoods. I assume this will just make iterations run more slowly, but otherwise things will still work (it seemed to when I just ran a toy model to estimate the overall mean).
> > > > 3. Lots of action in the transformed parameters block: the relationship between model parameters and the outputs that get entered in the likelihood is very complicated, and takes a while to compute. If this is what is causing things to crash, and if this might be solved by somehow pulling these calculations out separately in C++, I think its worth giving it a try.

> > > > My poorly-informed guess, as the model seems to run sometimes but not others, is that things are going awry when the sampler gets too far into the tail of the posterior. Does this sound possible?

Hi Daniel,

Thank you for laying this out so clearly. Sorry the simple model I sent did not work --> I forgot that you could specify simplex vectors, so instead that model had an awkward (and fatal, it seems) way of achieving the same result.

The suggestion of a Dirichlet is interesting. I raised a question about it earlier on this  <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/stan-users/bob$20multinomial$20dirichlet/stan-users/55-Dr6JW-yA/FQ2uwMtKd0cJ>thread, and went with the current approach as there seemed to be some trickiness involved with the Dirichlet, in that (if I am interpreting the comments and the manual correctly), the Dirichlet should really be taking the counts plus 1 as its argument (i.e. if one had integer data,  the likelihood of counts ~ Multinomial(theta) would be proportional to theta ~ Dirichlet(counts+1)). I guess this extra step really is a trivial problem, but please confirm that this step (add one to the counts) is needed.

Also, do you know if Dirichlet will be vectorised in Stan 2.0?  Presumably this would make Dirichlet the faster option as well.

For the transformed parameters section: I agree it is... busy. I need the detail to answer my research question, but there are many opportunities for bugs to come in. However, I have coded up a version in R and rcpp so will be able to use this to generate better inits (I think this has been a problem). This will also let me compare model results across R and Stan to check for bugs (I normally work in R so am more confident about spotting bugs there).

Also -- great idea about fake data, will give it a go.

Nick

On Tuesday, 1 October 2013 00:19:14 UTC-4, Daniel Lee wrote:
> Nick,
>
> Thanks for attaching the simple model. Unfortunately, I can't get it to work. I can't sample B1, B2, B3, B4 properly. I didn't want to spend too much time debugging what you have. Instead, I've created a model that works.
>
> My guess is that you really want the Dirichlet distribution instead of a multinomial -- that's from seeing the data and realizing your data are continuous. I'll write out both models, in case you have integer data. I've renamed the variables to something more general.
>
> Multinomial (discrete data)
> ------------------------------------
> data {
>   int <lower=0> N;
>   int ns[N,4];
> }
> parameters {
>   simplex[4] B;
> }
> model {
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     ns[n] ~ multinomial(B);
>   }
> }
>
> Dirichlet (continuous data)
> ------------------------------------
> data {
>   int <lower=0> N;
>   vector[4] ns[N];
> }
> parameters {
>   simplex[4] B;
> }
> model {
>   for (n in 1:N) {
>     B ~ dirichlet(ns[n]);
>   }
> }
>
> ------------------------------------
>
>
> First, notice the difference in data declaration. For multinomial, I've declared a 2D array of integers. For Dirichlet, it's a N-length array of 4-vectors.
>
> Second, I've gotten rid of the transformed data block. Here, you want to declare the B's in the original model as a simplex. There's no need to try to do any trickiness -- Stan can handle it all under the hood for you.
>
> If you wanted to try it out on more simple data first, you can replace the data block with a transformed data block like:
>
> transformed data {
>   int <lower=0> N;
>   vector[4] ns[100];
>   N <- 100;
>   for (n in 1:100) {
>     ns[n,1] <- 1;
>     ns[n,2] <- 10;
>     ns[n,3] <- 100;
>     ns[n,4] <- 1000;
>   }
> }
>
> Hopefully that helps and you can really simplify your model. If you want documentation on the distributions, you'll find them in the manual.
>
> When we suggest breaking down your model, these are sort of the steps we take. Even with the Dirichlet example, I put in fake data (as shown), where I knew the expected parameter values. I had original swapped the parameters and the variables since I was working with the multinomial first (written as 'ns[n] ~ dirichlet(B)') and it was clearly not right. I wouldn't have been able to pick that out if I used the full dataset to begin with. I also wouldn't have been able to debug it as quickly if there were lots of things happening in transformation blocks or restrictive priors. I guess I don't have the ability to intuit parameters through a thick model.
>
> Anyway, let us know how you get on with the rest of your model.
>
>
>
> Daniel
>

Thank you. This *does* work indeed. But in order to do this, most of my models have to be in a "transformed parameter" section (see attached file), which is somewhat counterintuitive. Ugly.

Yet another alternative could be to have (repeatable) "submodel" paragraphs, and a function to use their log_posterior in the main model. This could be worthwhile if one can factor the sampling along the same lines. But one can be afraid of some nasty side effects, such as the effects of "cut" in BUGS (Martyn Plummer insists on the fact that a Bugs program using cut is no longetr the representation of a distribution ; I think he's right).

> Dear list,
>
> I am trying to  duplicate Carlin & Chib (1995) results on the modelization of the compressive strength of Pines radiata wood by two linear regressio. This is easy to do. > The suggestion of a Dirichlet is interesting. I raised a question about it earlier on this

> and went with the current approach as there seemed to be some trickiness involved with the Dirichlet, in that (if I am

> interpreting the comments and the manual correctly), the Dirichlet should really be taking the counts */plus 1/* as its

> argument (i.e. if one had integer data,  the likelihood of counts ~ Multinomial(theta) would be proportional to theta ~
> Dirichlet(counts+1)). I guess this extra step really is a trivial problem, but please confirm that this step (add one to
> the counts) is needed.

The Stan parameterization of the Dirichlet is the usual one:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_distribution

You can see from the density that if the parameter vector is
all 1 values, it's a uniform prior.  So if you've seen 4 outcomes
of category 1, 3 of category 2 and 1 of category 3, and you
use a Dirichlet({1,1,1}) prior, then the posterior is
Dirichlet({5,4,2}), which is why I said the parameter is 1 plus
the prior number of observations in the doc.

> Also, do you know if Dirichlet will be vectorised in Stan 2.0?  Presumably this would make Dirichlet the faster option
> as well.

Not yet.  We're still working through the vectorization of
multivariates.  The metaprogramming's tricky, so we've been putting
it off.  But it's a high priority for us, so it'll be done soon
(by that, I mean probably over the next six months).

> For the transformed parameters section: I agree it is... busy. I need the detail to answer my research question, but
> there are many opportunities for bugs to come in. However, I have coded up a version in R and rcpp so will be able to
> use this to generate better inits (I think this has been a problem).

Reasonable inits help with convergence.

- Bob

Dear Bob,

Thank you for a prompt answer. I'll have to think a bit for a proper answer. Meanwhile, a couple of comments :

[ Snip...]

> This model reminds me we should check that all input characters
> are ASCII.  We don't explicitly support extended characters outside
> the ASCII range.  Presumably this just worked because you used
> the Latin1 encoding, and we're not checking the high bit.

Aauuuugh !  Accents and diacritical marks are *needed* for writing properly in almost any alphabetic language in the world (except modern English). I'm used to think in my mother language (except when I'm writing a paper), and I wouldn't like to be forced to think in English (or mutilated French or whatever), at least in my comments. Look at what the Germans did to their language to avoid typing ü or ß, and weep... And don't get me started about right-to-left languages (such as Hebrew and Arabic) or Asiatic (="ideopictograhic", "phonopictographic" or "mixed-grill") languages...

Couldn't Stan tolerate at least UTF-8 encoding of at least the comments ? Language lexical elements (identifiers !) are another matter, though... But it *is* possible. Exemple in R (3.0.1) :

> Sélénè<-"La lune"
> Λυσιστρατα<-"Quelle nana !"
> ls()
[1] "Sélénè"     "Λυσιστρατα"

[ re-Snip ]

> > which is somewhat counterintuitive. Furthermore, I do not think I can use the
> > "Var~whatever(Pars)" notation, and I have to use the less intuitive "lp__<-lp__+wwhatever_log(Var,Pars" notation.
>
> > Ugly.
>
> In Stan 2, the syntax is changing to "increment_log_prob(whatever_log(Var,Pars))"
>
> Still ugly, though.
>
> And allowing sampling statements in the transformed parameters
> block won't help with this, because it won't save the value.

Aaaargh ! We're back to square one : I want to save some intermediate results for further analysis. The only solution left (if I follow you correctly) is to declare them as transformed parameters *and recompute them* in the "generated quantities" paragraph.

Insane (and not necessarily possible if lp__ is involved)... <Sigh...>. Yes unctions would help (in the sense of avoiding cut't'paste, but not in terms of execution time) in this case. Somewhat.

Extending the scope of "model" variables is dirty, agreed. But much simpler, and, in my case, faster. Possibly add a modifier to the declaration to force the user to explicitly allow this scope extension (such as "exported real foo;" instead of "real foo;") ?

>
> The other thing to be careful about is that the ~ and <- have
> slightly different interpretations.  The sampling statements
> drop constant terms, because we only need the log probability up
> to a constant factor.  The explicit _log forms do not drop any
> terms.

This I'm aware of. The same kind of (over-)simplification also happens in R (e. g. lmer (lme4) and lm (stats) do not produce a *real* deviance, but a deviance "up to a constant", which makes them incomparable (the constant is not the same)... Ouch !

>
> > Yet another alternative could be to have (repeatable) "submodel" paragraphs, and a function to use their log_posterior
> > in the main model. This could be worthwhile if one can factor the sampling along the same lines.
>
> Could you write out what you think this'd look like?

There, I have to think. I have a clear idea of what I want to do *now*, but quite unsure of the possible other uses. See below.

>
> We've been thinking about adding functions with and without
> return types.

Please do that. I've cursed BUGS and its authors to the seventh generation times and again for not having even macroes (even reverted to Metropolis-Hastings written in R to avoid tedious cut'n'paste'n'fix'n'correct'n'wail...). But I was thinking of something else, which is not yet crystal-clear to me...

>  But I'm not sure how this would help here.
> Maybe something like:
>
>     log probability foo(vector[] x, vector[] y, real alpha, real beta, real<lower=0> sigma) {
>       for (n in 1:size(x))
>         y[n] ~ normal(x[n] * alpha + beta, sigma);
>     }

That is a classical function. Yes, it would help.  Tremendously in some cases. But since Stan is lacking (as almost any C-derived language) an "amorphous collection" type such a list, this is somewhat restrictive...

Saint John MacCarthy, ora pro nobis...

> Then if you did:
>
>    lp_temp <- foo(x,y,alpha,beta,sigma);
>
> you might get what you want.
>
>  > But one can be afraid
> > of some nasty side effects, such as the effects of "cut" in BUGS (Martyn Plummer insists on the fact that a Bugs program
> > using cut is no longetr the representation of a distribution ; I think he's right).
>
> If we did this in Stan, it wouldn't behave like BUGS's cut.
> It would behave like it was a macro (only with proper scope).

With related (but not identical) problems  about what exactly the resulting program implements...

>
>
> Martyn's right that using cut changes the interpretation of a program.
> The uses I've mainly seen is to do some predictive inference using
> the fitted parameters that does not feed back into model estimation.
> In this case, the parameters still get the right distribution, but the
> inference isn't full Bayes (though in some cases it'll give you the
> same answer).

This kind of inference is sometimes much more important for  decision-making than strict Bayesian inference about the model. Think medicine. Think policy making (uh oh...). Think politics (yuck !). Strict Bayesian inference is needed when one have an epistemic problem ; prediction is often more useful in pragmatic problems (especially in the short range).

Again, thank you or your help !
>
> - Bob
- Emmanuel

> Aauuuugh !  Accents and diacritical marks are *needed* for writing properly in almost any alphabetic language in the
> world (except modern English).

Yes, and Chinese characters are needed for Chinese, and so on.
It's a huge mess.  My own background's in natural language processing,
and I've spent a crazy-large amount of time dealing with broken character
encoding issues.  In fact, my wife and I have a book coming out soon on
how to deal with encodings in Java!

> I'm used to think in my mother language (except when I'm writing a paper), and I wouldn't
> like to be forced to think in English (or mutilated French or whatever), at least in my comments. Look at what the
> Germans did to their language to avoid typing ü or ß, and weep... And don't get me started about right-to-left languages
> (such as Hebrew and Arabic) or Asiatic (="ideopictograhic", "phonopictographic" or "mixed-grill") languages...

Right-to-left (or top-to-bottom) rendering is a completely separate issue
from character encodings.   The order of rendering is not part of the
Unicode standard per se, but instead a directive to something like a web
browser.  Arabic's especially fun because numbers and quoted English words
go left-to-right, whereas Arabic characters go right-to-left.

> Couldn't Stan tolerate at least UTF-8 encoding of at least the comments ?

Not without a huge amount of work.  C++ doesn't have the nice
built-ins that Java has for dealing with Unicode.

But part of the problem is that users are terrible at being consistent
with anything but ASCII.  I've gotten mixed docs of Latin1 and UTF-8
that people have munged together in Perl or Python.

A document has to be encoding in a single encoding.  So we can't do
something different for comments than other code.

We could eventually add UTF-8 support, but given everything else we
have to do, it's just not a high priority.

> Language lexical elements (identifiers !) are
> another matter, though... But it *is* possible.

Of course.  Java lets you write Unicode in your programs.  But
then you have to be careful to declare the encoding, as the default
is just by operating system and configuration.

> Exemple in R (3.0.1) :
>
> |
>  > Sélénè<-"La lune"
>  > Λυσιστρατα<-"Quelle nana !"
>  > ls()
> [1] "Sélénè"     "Λυσιστρατα"

> left (if I follow you correctly) is to declare them as transformed parameters *and recompute them* in the "generated

You don't need to recompute them.  Transformed parameters
are visible in the generated quantities block.

The problem is that you may not care about writing them out if
you need a lot of them.

> Insane (and not necessarily possible if lp__ is involved)... <Sigh...>. Yes unctions would help (in the sense of
> avoiding cut't'paste, but not in terms of execution time) in this case. Somewhat.

I'm not sure what you are saying is insane.

> Extending the scope of "model" variables is dirty, agreed. But much simpler, and, in my case, faster. Possibly add a
> modifier to the declaration to force the user to explicitly allow this scope extension (such as "exported real foo;"
> instead of "real foo;") ?

We're trying to skate a thin line between making Stan expressive
but not too complicated.  As soon as you start adding namespaces
and things like this, you start losing non-programmers (and even
some programmers).

But I'm not sure what you're suggesting anyway.

>     The other thing to be careful about is that the ~ and <- have
>     slightly different interpretations.  The sampling statements
>     drop constant terms, because we only need the log probability up
>     to a constant factor.  The explicit _log forms do not drop any
>     terms.

> produce a *real* deviance, but a deviance "up to a constant", which makes them incomparable (the constant is not the
> same)... Ouch !

In retrospect, we should probably allow a way for the user
to control this both ways.  In the C++ API, whether or not to
compute up to a constant is a template parameter.

>      > Yet another alternative could be to have (repeatable) "submodel" paragraphs, and a function to use their
>     log_posterior
>      > in the main model. This could be worthwhile if one can factor the sampling along the same lines.
>
>     Could you write out what you think this'd look like?
>
>

Starting from examples is good.

>     We've been thinking about adding functions with and without
>     return types.
>
>
> Please do that. I've cursed BUGS and its authors to the seventh generation times and again for not having even macroes
> (even reverted to Metropolis-Hastings written in R to avoid tedious cut'n'paste'n'fix'n'correct'n'wail...). But I was
> thinking of something else, which is not yet crystal-clear to me...

ones that return values and increment lp__.  We haven't
been thinking along the lines you are suggesting for saving
lp calculations, which is why I was asking what exactly you
wanted to do.

>       But I'm not sure how this would help here.

>          log probability foo(vector[] x, vector[] y, real alpha, real beta, real<lower=0> sigma) {

>          }
>
>
> That is a classical function. Yes, it would help.  Tremendously in some cases. But since Stan is lacking (as almost any
> C-derived language) an "amorphous collection" type such a list, this is somewhat restrictive...

Yes, more general lists are also on the to-do list.  Again,
we're not exactly sure what the design should be for them.

We're particularly keen to get some notion of ragged arrays.

One of the reasons R is so slow and wasteful of memory is the
generic data types.

> Saint John MacCarthy, ora pro nobis...

You could always try the Church sampler.  It's basically
Scheme.

>     Then if you did:
>
>         lp_temp <- foo(x,y,alpha,beta,sigma);
>
>     you might get what you want.
>
>       > But one can be afraid
>      > of some nasty side effects, such as the effects of "cut" in BUGS (Martyn Plummer insists on the fact that a Bugs
>     program
>      > using cut is no longetr the representation of a distribution ; I think he's right).
>
>     If we did this in Stan, it wouldn't behave like BUGS's cut.
>     It would behave like it was a macro (only with proper scope).
>
>
> With related (but not identical) problems  about what exactly the resulting program implements...

In BUGS's defense, there is a spec for what it does.
And there's always an issue of what code does.  I don't see
how this is any different.

>     Martyn's right that using cut changes the interpretation of a program.
>     The uses I've mainly seen is to do some predictive inference using
>     the fitted parameters that does not feed back into model estimation.
>     In this case, the parameters still get the right distribution, but the
>     inference isn't full Bayes (though in some cases it'll give you the
>     same answer).
>
>
> This kind of inference is sometimes much more important for  decision-making than strict Bayesian inference about the
> model. Think medicine. Think policy making (uh oh...). Think politics (yuck !). Strict Bayesian inference is needed when
> one have an epistemic problem ; prediction is often more useful in pragmatic problems (especially in the short range).

You can take this up with the Bayesians :-)

The usual motiviation in my experience is either (a) confusion about
what constitutes "cheating" (specifically, can you update the model with
respect to the "test" data, or do you have to fix a model based on "training"
data), or (b)  (b) an efficiency issue (specifically when you have to do a lot
of prediction and don't have time or expertise to update the model.
My impression was that BUGS used cut mainly for (b), and I assume that's
what you're talking about in medical decision problems (that is, you don't
want the doctor making decisions to have to update the model as they go;  but
of course, they do this informally anyway).

- Bob

As I said in the last message, I think we should be OK
with comments in UTF-8, but if we allow variable names to
be UTF-8 (or UTF-16 big endian, or whatever), then there's
the issue of making the toolchain (shell, R or Python,
etc.) compatible.  It's a real pain setting up Unicode in
Windows (don't get me started on Windows bastardized
Latin character sets).

More below.

On 10/3/13 1:23 AM, Emmanuel Charpentier wrote:

>

>
>     Not without a huge amount of work.  C++ doesn't have the nice
>     built-ins that Java has for dealing with Unicode.
>
>
> Perfect illustration of the US-ASCII-slanted infrastructure.

There's just ASCII, not a special US version.  And I think
it started that way because of the early computer development
here and in the UK.

>     But part of the problem is that users are terrible at being consistent
>     with anything but ASCII.  I've gotten mixed docs of Latin1 and UTF-8
>     that people have munged together in Perl or Python.
>
>
> Indeed. Even with a UFT-8 installation (Linux, using FR_fr UTF8 locale), UTF-8 editors (emacs) , I seem to have managed
> (how ?) to send to the list a Latin-1-encoded example... (Apologies or that, by the way...).

No idea what happens in mailers.  That's one source of text
issues I haven't explored.

>     A document has to be encoding in a single encoding.  So we can't do
>     something different for comments than other code.
>
>     We could eventually add UTF-8 support, but given everything else we
>     have to do, it's just not a high priority.
>
>
> My point is that nowadays, using Unicode or one of its subsets should *not* require any special thought. We are dragging
> a lot of baggage (libraries, compilers, basic utilities...) built on the "Anything is 7-bits ASCII" assumption...

The problem is that there are multiple encodings for Unicode,
and when you go from 8-bit to 16-bit (which is more efficient
for anything with many non-ASCII characters), then you have
endian issues and byte-order issues.

- Bob

I've thought about it a bit more and non-ASCII comments
are OK, as long as the char encoding encodes ASCII as ASCII
(i.e., the code points below 128 match ASCII and ASCII
is encoded as bytes).  This includes ASCII, Latin1,
other Latin-X, Win-1252, and the UTF-8 encoding of Unicode.

etc.  For instance, UTF-16 matches ASCII on code points, but
uses 16-bit output padded for ASCII.

the actual sampler and working with Peter Li on the model encodings.

It looked to me like you were trying to save the log
probability values.  Sampling statements don't assign
log probabilities, they just increment the underlying
log probability accumulator.  So if I do y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma),
there's no way to save the state.

The basic idea is that a Stan model is just defining a log
probability.  Sampling statements increment it, and you can increment
it directly.  Only the log probability affects the sampling,
which is defined over the parameters.  Everything else is
derived from that.  So you can work with transformed parameters,
but they're derived from parameters and data.  Similarly with
generated quantities, but the generated quantities don't affect
sampling at all --- they're like the "cut" part of BUGS, though

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] determining memory usage
messages.body_plain:
R will auto-expand memory until you don't have
any more.

If you save in RStan directly rather than writing out
to a file, then I think it'll take at least 8 bytes per
parameter (count cells in matrices, etc.) per iteration, and maybe
there's a factor of 2 in there for peak memory usage (I'm not
following exactly).  And it'll take 8 bytes per data value.
Then there's some overhead for R itself, which you can
measure when R starts up and will depend on whether you're
running 32-bit or 64-bit R.

If you stream out to a CSV file, there's no per-parameter
overhead (besided a little bit used in the leapfrog steps,
maybe the equivalent of 10 iterations worth).

messages.body_plain:
A very big mess.  C++11 is still trickling out to projects
like R.  And that Wikipedia section doesn't say how you
set the compilers to interpret actual UTF-8, UTF-16 or
UTF-32 characters that occur in programs (it's just a flag
in Java, so presumably you can do this in C++ --- it's just
one more thing that can fail to be connected together
properly).

I'm not worried about dealing with the encodings on the Stan
side --- I know how to deal with encodings (I used to do natural
language processing, where it's very important).  It's just the
very error prone when you have to integrate text editors, shells,
various R interfaces, and then you get variations across operating
systems and locales.  We thought we'd just reduce the total number
of potential headaches at the risk of pissing off non-English
writers.

When you say "Debian went with UTF-8", what does that mean?
Unix is still underlying bytes.  Programming languages and applications
can still do whatever they want with the bytes.  Does it just mean
that's what the shell expects to render if it sees standard output?
Or what GUI elements expect in their displays?

- Bob

I think the effect is supposed to be pervasive.  For source packages,
it means text files like changes, README, licenses are in UTF-8.  So
contributors with names that have non-ASCII characters can put their
names in those files.  For the terminal it means accepting and
rendering non-ASCII.

messages.subject: Problem with a simple mixture of normals.
messages.subject_clean: Problem with a simple mixture of normals.
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

I am trying to attack the problem studied by Carlin & Chib (1995) in the first part of their paper. This has given the "Pines" example in vol III of BUGS examples. It is a simple linear regression problem of a dependent variable Y on either X or Z, closely related continuous variables. In order to compare the merits of those fits, Carlin & Chib introduce a "state" variable stating at each iteration of the sampler which of the models will be used. The posterior distribution of pi gives an idea of the relative strength of the models (about the same meaning as the Bayes factor).

I'm trying to fit Y by a mixture of regression of X and Z.

A first model (M1.stan) just fits these two models, with no difficulty whatsoever. However, I find myself unable to fit to a mixture (M2.stant ; I followed the mixture example of the Stan user's guide), and am unable to understand why. I get tons of "Metropolis rejection" messages and get four chains with no movement at all, except when I try to specify 'init="random", which quickly gives me :
"Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the model."

Replacing "log_sum_exp(lp1+log(pi), lp2+log(1.0-pi))" by the equivalent but numerically unstable "log(pi*exp(lp1)+(1.0-pi)*exp(lp2))" quickly converges ... to nonsensical values !

I am at the end of my rope here... Can someone suggest something ? I think I'm missing an important point.

Newbie, take a look at the manual and make sure things are parameterized properly. For example, the equivalent prior on the tau's is:
tau[j] ~ normal(0, 10);

not:
tau[j] ~ normal(0, 0.1);

Stan parameterizes the normal distribution with mean and standard deviation.

I'm not sure of the other differences in parameterization between Stan and JAGS. After double-checking the model, can you report whether you get similar results?

Daniel

Hi all,

I'm doing a kind of semi-supervised regression. The code and toy data
are at: https://gist.github.com/danstowell/6828740

With this code (in stan 1.3), I'm getting a lot of errors with NaN
values, preventing it from running:

"""
Iteration:    1 / 2000 [  0%]  (Adapting)
alpha: 3.76273:0
sigma: 1e-06:0
tendencies_alpha: [1.73544:0,0.618637:0,0.553649:0,0.529565:0]
tendencies_beta:  [0.5:0,0.5:0,0.5:0,0.5:0]

Informational Message: The parameter state is about to be Metropolis
rejected due to the following underlying, non-fatal (really) issue
(and please ignore that what comes next might say 'error'): Error in
function stan::prob::exponential_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Random
variable is nan:0, but must not be nan!
If the problem persists across multiple draws, you might have a
problem with an initial state or a gradient somewhere.
 If the problem does not persist, the resulting samples will still be
drawn from the posterior.
"""
(...this message then repeats a lot, until fail.)

If you comment out the exponential priors, you get a similar message
except that the choking happens in beta_log() instead.

I'm scratching my head about these errors because all my parameters
are fairly narrowly constrained, initialised humanely, and as far as I
can tell there's no log(0)... so I don't see where the nans are coming
from!

Thanks for any thoughts you can offer.

Best
Dan
--
http://www.mcld.co.uk

messages.subject_clean: big multinomial: simpler not better
messages.body_plain:
My collaborators were not wild about a model with a lot of interactions,
so I tried a much simpler one.  The original interacted almost every
variable with respondent race and HIV status (3 levels of each).  The
outcome had 5 levels.  The only interactions in the new model were a few
interactions with race.

The simpler model behaves worse than the more complex one; in fact, it
behaves very badly.

I'm a little puzzled that this is happening.  Though I thought the more
complex model would capture the data better, most of the coefficients it
estimated were quite small.  Even if they weren't the behavior is
suprising to me.

I wonder if anyone has any comments about what these results might indicate.

DETAILS

The new model allowed the 2-way coefficients to have a different
variance than the lower order ones.

messages.body_plain:
On 10/3/13 3:31 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> On Thu, Oct 03, 2013 at 03:20:10PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>>
>> When you say "Debian went with UTF-8", what does that mean?
>> Unix is still underlying bytes.  Programming languages and applications
>> can still do whatever they want with the bytes.  Does it just mean
>> that's what the shell expects to render if it sees standard output?
>> Or what GUI elements expect in their displays?

> I think the effect is supposed to be pervasive.  For source packages,
> it means text files like changes, README, licenses are in UTF-8.  So
> contributors with names that have non-ASCII characters can put their
> names in those files.  For the terminal it means accepting and
> rendering non-ASCII.

It can only be pervasive at the OS interface level.  These are
all under the OS's control.  I find the UTF-8-based shell in the
Mac OS to be really useful.

Programs themselves are still going to operate at the byte level
when they open up files to read.  If those bytes represent characters,
their character encoding needs to be specified.  Which is a huge pain
and very error prone.  An example is a web browser --- it reads
data from HTTP connections (underlyingly, just another stream like
a file, only with some formatting specified by standard), then renders
it.  It's the browser's job to convert from bytes to characters.

...

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Other than the typo, the way you're coding mixtures looks
OK to me.

There's always a problem with mixtures in that they can wander
off into very low variance solutions.  (Where one mixture component
accounts for one data point with zero variance.)

What happens if you tighten up the priors around the parameters
to near where you want them to be?

When you say the distribution of pi is flat, you mean pi = 0.5?

- Bob

P.S.  You don't need the truncations on truncations with constant
parameters.

   s~cauchy(0, 5) T[0,];
   t~cauchy(0, 5) T[0,];

You also don't need the uniform on pi.

P.P.S.  For arithmetic stability and speed, there's also a
         log1m(u) == log(1 - u) function, that you can use
         in place of log(1 - pi).

messages.body_plain:
On Fri, Oct 04, 2013 at 08:09:52PM -0400, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Q1:  If you have parameters and interacted parameters, will
> you generally have all the parameters being smaller?
>
> Q2:  If so, should you then have smaller prior scales for the
> lower-level parameters?

The models I was using grouped the coefficients into batches, each of
which had its own scale.  Loosely, the batches were based on the
order of the term, e.g., 3 way interactions were in one batch, 2 way
another, and so on.

sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5)  //sigma a vector
beta[i] ~ normal(0, sigma[sdclass[i]])
where sdclass gives the group that beta[i] is in.

Also, parameterization used R's contr.sum, so that the sum of effects
across levels is 0.  I thought that might help with the scaling if the
higher order interactions were smaller.

>
> Q3:  Is there some way to keep the expected sizes of the
> basic parameters the same so that the higher-level parameters
> just take up the slack?

Does the contr.sum coding address that?

>
> I'm probably not asking this the right way, but I hope people
> know what I mean.

I'm not sure I follow, in particular about why it matters if the
scales are smaller or larger.

I think you are comparing estimates for A in 2 models:
I) y ~ A + B  (R notation for y as a function of 2 main effects)
II) y ~ A + B + A:B  (A:B is the interaction).

and then you are asking about the magnitude of the effects estimated
for the A term in I and II.

Ross

messages.subject: abs vs. fabs; auto-casting real to int is dangerous
messages.subject_clean: abs vs. fabs; auto-casting real to int is dangerous
messages.body_plain:
I just literally spent two days tracking down why posterior predictions in my model were not what a parallel computation in R thought they should be.

Turns out abs(real x) actually computes floor(abs(x)) because "abs" is for integers and "fabs" is for floats and, "abs" on a real value apparently casts to int first.

This is bizarre. I can tolerate there being different functions for integer and float, but in that case it should be an error to call abs() on a real value. For it to auto-cast to int is asking for problems.

Can there be some documentation in the User's guide on the difference between abs(real x) and fabs(real x)?

Better yet, can there be better behavior when auto-casting (such as warning when implicit real->int casts discard fractional parts?)

Peter

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Same initialisation values
messages.body_plain:
That depends on who you ask :-)

We like to recommend that you start with more diffuse
initial points to make sure that the initial points have
been "forgotten".  Otherwise, you might think you've converged
when you haven't.

Others might recommend you just run one chain for a very very
very very very very long time.  The point is that asymptotically
the result's the same :-)

Having said that, you often need to initialize with a single
reasonable value just for convenience.

In the future, we want to add a controllable bit of randomization
around a user-specified initialization point.  The problem with
doing this yourself is that you need to respect the constraints.
We can just work on the unconstrained scale internally the way we
do for default inits.

- Bob

>     What happens if you tighten up the priors around the parameters
>     to near where you want them to be?
>

> Ditto,with slightly lesser variances. Traces show that chains converge on *different* central values for the variance
> parameters.

Any idea if the posterior is multimodal?  MCMC methods
can get stuck around local modes.

>     When you say the distribution of pi is flat, you mean pi = 0.5?
>
>
> No, I mean almost uniform(0,1)

That sounds like something's not connected.

>     - Bob
>
>     P.S.  You don't need the truncations on truncations with constant
>     parameters.
>
>         s~cauchy(0, 5) T[0,];
>         t~cauchy(0, 5) T[0,];
>
>
> Reminds myelf that s and t are variance parameters... Is there a computational cost for this truncation ?

Short answer: yes, but it shouldn't be too bad if there
aren't that many calls.

Longer answer:  We haven't linked the truncation and the distribution
syntax, so the truncation can't figure out that it's not needed here,
so it'll get calculated.  Having said that, it only gets calculated with
real (internally double) values, so there's no hit on memory or on
auto-diff time.

>
>     You also don't need the uniform on pi.
>
>
> More of a placeholder for a future dirichlet prior on more than two models.

The Stan translator's smart enough to optimize everything
away it can --- what's left are bounds checks.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] abs vs. fabs; auto-casting real to int is dangerous
messages.body_plain:
On 10/4/13 10:38 PM, Peter Meilstrup wrote:
> I just literally spent two days tracking down why posterior predictions in my model were not what a parallel computation
> in R thought they should be.

I'm truly sorry to hear that.  Thanks so much for reporting this calmly
and not yelling at us.

> Turns out abs(real x) actually computes floor(abs(x)) because "abs" is for integers and "fabs" is for floats and, "abs"
> on a real value apparently casts to int first.

This is a bug, not our intention.

> This is bizarre. I can tolerate there being different functions for integer and float, but in that case it should be an
> error to call abs() on a real value. For it to auto-cast to int is asking for problems.

I agree.  The problem is that C++ is bringing in the
standard library definition of abs(int) and applying it
by casting the double to an int.  Our implementation will
do the right thing for parameter real, just not data real
values.

> Can there be some documentation in the User's guide on the difference between abs(real x) and fabs(real x)?

Doc isn't enough.

> Better yet, can there be better behavior when auto-casting (such as warning when implicit real->int casts discard
> fractional parts?)

Yes.  The current behavior's a bug as is the current doc
for not at least indicating our intention that abs(real) and
fabs(real) do the same thing.

I created a simple replicable example of the bug and included
it in the issue I just put in our issue tracker:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/257

This is very high priority and will definitely go in before 2.0.

I'm torn between the two solutions listed in the issue:

1.  Try to get abs(real) do the same thing as fabs(real).

2.  Remove abs(real) altogether.

I like 2 better, but I worry about backward compatiblity.

Best is probably:

3.  Follow (1) and at same time deprecate use of abs(real)

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
On 10/6/13 9:06 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> What if UTF-8 was encoded using percent-encoding or punycode? Which would be
> better for C++?
>
> - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent_encoding#Current_standard
> - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punycode
>
> I think it would be great to be able to write: 标准差 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5)

I think it'll introduce too many errors!  Especially if we
add another layer of escaping.  The problem is more in transport
to and from interfaces like R, Python, the shell, and text
editors than within a file itself.

If we do support Unicode, then the whole doc should be in Unicode.
XML does this the right way.  Note there's no way to declare the
encoding and still have the doc be in that encoding, because you
get a chicken and egg problem.  So this means external specifications
of character encoding, which means things can break.

Or we could just insist on UTF-8, which is at least ASCII compatible.
I don't know if it's compatible with everyone's text editors.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Stan is ASCII only
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Stan is ASCII only
messages.body_plain:
Insisting on UTF8 over other input encodings is extremely sensible. All ASCII input (and thus all current Stan code) is valid UTF8; there are large classes of errors (like endian reversal, or mistaking code points for code units) that simply can't happen in UTF8, and it's the default encoding for many tools. Also, since it's most common character encoding on the Web by far [1], it's highly likely that a text editor will support it properly. (Old versions of Notepad may be a notable exception.)

[1] http://w3techs.com/technologies/overview/character_encoding/all

>From a brief skim, this might be helpful for the compiler-writers: http://www.utf8everywhere.org/

Compiling the resulting code is, unfortunately, a more complicated story, as I'm forced to conclude after lots of digging. g++ (probably 4.2+) supports the "experimental" '-fextended-identifiers' option, letting you encode your variable names with \u... or \U... [1] [2], and I tested this works with Stan-generated code. But extended identifier support only came to clang in version 3.3 [3], which is newer than /usr/bin/clang on my OS X Mountain Lion system. Promisingly, though, "/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents//Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/clang++" (from Xcode 5) is 3.3, though, and it successfully compiles my UTF-8 encoded Stan source file with no problem -- both with and without \u-encoding the characters. I don't know anything about MSVC.

[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2681778/g-unicode-variable-name
[2] http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Preprocessor-Options.html
[3] http://llvm.org/releases/3.3/tools/clang/docs/ReleaseNotes.html

Neither punycode nor percent-encoding produce valid C++ identifiers, unfortunately, though I now appreciate the sentiment behind that suggestion :) I almost suggested Base64-encoded UTF8, until I realized that it needs '.' or ':' or '+' (even though you can get away with omitting the '='s). An ugly stopgap would be: non-ASCII variable names get encoded as '_U' followed by their (4-byte) code points in hex.

Hope this helps,
-Ken

Thanks for the overview, Kenneth.  Your post supports
my contention that it's complicated!

I hadn't realized clang++ wasn't there in terms of support
until 3.3.  We want to at least support the standard Mac OS and
Linux distributions of clang++ because they compile so much faster.

We're OK on comments because those don't get written through into
the C++.

I'm guessing that the \u is for literals, not for variable
names?  It would be awful if you needed an ASCII wart for
variable name escaping.

As to editors, Aquamacs on Mac OS supports unicode, as does
Gnu Emacs on Windows.   I don't know what the status is on
Xemacs --- I stopped using it ages ago when I needed Unicode
and it didn't support it :-)

We're about to mangle local variables in the programs to
deal with conflicts with functions (we don't want future functions
breaking backward compatibility).  But mangling to and from UTF-8
would be too much work.

- Bob

The problem is that you're sending in values of 1 to
a beta distribution, which returns -infinity.  It's support
is only on the open interval (0,1).

You can see it with these prints inside your M_trn loop:

     print("proby_trn[",m,"]=",proby_trn[m]);
     print("tendencies_alpha=",tendencies_alpha,"; tendencies_beta=",tendencies_beta);
     print("beta, m=", m, "; log prob=", beta_log(proby_trn[m], tendencies_alpha, tendencies_beta));

So it's a problem with data, not with inits.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Stan is ASCII only
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

So I take it it's not a matter of simply switching from std::string to
std::wstring? (I know only enough C++ to injure myself.)

PyStan could support a switch to anything (utf-8, utf-16/UCS-2) in a pinch.  It
already explicitly encodes strings to ascii when they are passed to Stan (via
std::string).

Best,

Allen

On 10/07, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks for the overview, Kenneth.  Your post supports
> my contention that it's complicated!
>
> I hadn't realized clang++ wasn't there in terms of support
> until 3.3.  We want to at least support the standard Mac OS and
> Linux distributions of clang++ because they compile so much faster.
>
> We're OK on comments because those don't get written through into
> the C++.
>
> I'm guessing that the \u is for literals, not for variable
> names?  It would be awful if you needed an ASCII wart for
> variable name escaping.
>
> As to editors, Aquamacs on Mac OS supports unicode, as does
> Gnu Emacs on Windows.   I don't know what the status is on
> Xemacs --- I stopped using it ages ago when I needed Unicode
> and it didn't support it :-)
>
> We're about to mangle local variables in the programs to
> deal with conflicts with functions (we don't want future functions
> breaking backward compatibility).  But mangling to and from UTF-8
> would be too much work.
>
> - Bob
>
> On 10/7/13 1:20 AM, Kenneth Arnold wrote:
> >Insisting on UTF8 over other input encodings is extremely sensible. All ASCII input (and thus all current Stan code) is
> >valid UTF8; there are large classes of errors (like endian reversal, or mistaking code points for code units) that
> >simply can't happen in UTF8, and it's the default encoding for many tools. Also, since it's most common character
> >encoding on the Web by far [1], it's highly likely that a text editor will support it properly. (Old versions of Notepad
> >may be a notable exception.)
> >
> >[1] http://w3techs.com/technologies/overview/character_encoding/all
> >
> > From a brief skim, this might be helpful for the compiler-writers: http://www.utf8everywhere.org/
> >
> >Compiling the resulting code is, unfortunately, a more complicated story, as I'm forced to conclude after lots of
> >digging. g++ (probably 4.2+) supports the "experimental" '-fextended-identifiers' option, letting you encode your
> >variable names with \u... or \U... [1] [2], and I tested this works with Stan-generated code. But extended identifier
> >support only came to clang in version 3.3 [3], which is newer than /usr/bin/clang on my OS X Mountain Lion system.
> >Promisingly, though, "/Applications/Xcode.app/Contents//Developer/Toolchains/XcodeDefault.xctoolchain/usr/bin/clang++"
> >(from Xcode 5) is 3.3, though, and it successfully compiles my UTF-8 encoded Stan source file with no problem -- both
> >with and without \u-encoding the characters. I don't know anything about MSVC.
> >
> >[1] http://stackoverflow.com/questions/2681778/g-unicode-variable-name
> >[2] http://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Preprocessor-Options.html
> >[3] http://llvm.org/releases/3.3/tools/clang/docs/ReleaseNotes.html
> >
> >Neither punycode nor percent-encoding produce valid C++ identifiers, unfortunately, though I now appreciate the
> >sentiment behind that suggestion :) I almost suggested Base64-encoded UTF8, until I realized that it needs '.' or ':' or
> >'+' (even though you can get away with omitting the '='s). An ugly stopgap would be: non-ASCII variable names get
> >encoded as '_U' followed by their (4-byte) code points in hex.
> >
> >Hope this helps,
> >-Ken
> >
> >
> >On Sun, Oct 6, 2013 at 9:22 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com <mailto:ca...@alias-i.com>> wrote:
> >
> >
> >
> >    On 10/6/13 9:06 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> >
> >        What if UTF-8 was encoded using percent-encoding or punycode? Which would be
> >        better for C++?
> >
> >        - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percent_encoding#Current_standard
> >        - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punycode
> >
> >        I think it would be great to be able to write: 标准差 ~ cauchy(0, 2.5)
> >
> >
> >    I think it'll introduce too many errors!  Especially if we
> >    add another layer of escaping.  The problem is more in transport
> >    to and from interfaces like R, Python, the shell, and text
> >    editors than within a file itself.
> >
> >    If we do support Unicode, then the whole doc should be in Unicode.
> >    XML does this the right way.  Note there's no way to declare the
> >    encoding and still have the doc be in that encoding, because you
> >    get a chicken and egg problem.  So this means external specifications
> >    of character encoding, which means things can break.
> >
> >    Or we could just insist on UTF-8, which is at least ASCII compatible.
> >    I don't know if it's compatible with everyone's text editors.
> >
> >    - Bob
> >

messages.subject: Issues compiling simple model for custom exponential (user guide example)
messages.subject_clean: Issues compiling simple model for custom exponential (user guide example)
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,
I've just stated using Stan, and I have been running through some examples in the Stan user guide. In the user guide, it indicates that a custom probability function can be made. The second example (pg 115) is to replace

x ~ exponential(lambda);

with

lp__ <- lp__ + log(lambda) - y * lambda;

However, when I try this, I get the following error:

Error in stanc(file = file, model_code = model_code, model_name = model_name,  :
  failed to parse Stan model 'simpleex3' with error message:
EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=12, column=44

        lp__ <- lp__ + log(lambda) - x * lambda;
                                           ^-- here

Everything runs fine if I use the standard exponential function, but not the custom one. I imagine I'm missing something rather simple - could someone help me understand what the issue is?  R code, model, and error message attached.

Thanks in advance,
Ryan

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan,

If you read the error message, it states:

    DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
    no matches for function name="multiply"
        arg 0 type=real[1]

This is trying to let you know that multiplication isn't vectorized. That is, the first argument, x, can't be an array. (x is defined as "real x[N]", which is showing up as "type=real[1]" in the parser.)

The fix is simple. Replace the single, vectorized call with a loop. The original line:

    lp__ <- lp__ + log(lambda) - x * lambda;

The fixed lines:

    for (n in 1:N) {
      lp__ <- lp__ + log(lambda) - x[n] * lambda;
    }

Daniel

PS. The files were attached, but Bob's email program may have eaten them.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Using uninitialized variables
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Using uninitialized variables
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I just wanted to chime in to say that I experienced a similar initialization problem.  I hope this note may be useful to others who encounter similar errors.

I had declared a convenience variable (real scalar) in my model section, which was supposed to be assigned a value via a series of conditional statements and then used to calculate the likelihood.  Because I mistakenly used only strict inequalities in the conditionals, the variable was never initialized in certain edge cases (i.e. where > ... and < ... both evaluated to false).  This resulted in stan segfaulting.

In retrospect, the error stan fails with (below) was actually fairly informative, in that it suggests a null pointer which was references by the non-initialized variable:

Signal: Segmentation fault (11)
Signal code: Address not mapped (1)
Failing at address: 0x8

But it took me a great deal of debugging trial and error (and, critically, the help of Dougal Sutherland :) to identify the culprit variable.

My thanks to all of the Stan team for this fantastic package!

Best,

~Nathan

messages.body_plain:
Some comments below, but you really need Matt or Michael
helping with this one.  Or maybe Andrew's had some experience
with hierarchical Student-t priors.

On 10/10/13 2:19 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> I tried estimating some models using a student t instead of a normal.
> The was to match my expectation that most effects would be ~0, but a few
> might be notable.
>
> It didn't work too well.  I wonder if part of the problem is that the
> specification of a variable df undercuts the Matt trick, since even the
> _raw parameters are now changing scale.

As Matt likes to say, that was "a Matt trick", not "the Matt trick".
I don't know how well it'll work here, but you can take the Student-t
apart into component normal and chi-square distributions:

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Student's_t-distribution#As_the_distribution_of_a_test_statistic

Another Matt trick did the same kind of thing for gamma distributions.

> Is there anything to that?  Is there a way around it, for example
> altering the sd of the _raw distribution to offset the scale changes
> induced by the df?  Unfortunately that isn't possible for df<2 (since t
> has no finite variance there).  Maybe restrict df to be >2?

If you make df big enough, you're back to roughly normal :-)

> Some details:
>
> First try: fix df for t at 1.  A total disaster: after 7 hours I had a
> minimum n_eff of 2!

I'm not sure why that would be so problematic.  Fixing df=1 just
gives you the Cauchy distribution.    But even there, the sampler
can wander off into the tails, which have a rather different scale
for the Cauchy than the central part.   Did the traceplots wander up into
high values?

> Second try: allow df to have a cauchy(0, 5) prior.  This took only 0.3
> hours, but n_eff was only 24 (and this from 3000 iterations
> post-warmup).

If that's as bad as it gets, that's about an hour and fifteen
minutes to get 100 effective samples.

Were the results sensible?

> The estimation code for the second try included this (excerpts only)
> parameters {
>      matrix[J, K] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
>      real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
>      vector<lower=0>[NSD] df; // df for t distn
> }
> transformed parameters {
>      matrix [J, K] beta;
>      for(ir in 1:J)
>         beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
> }
> model {
>      sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>      df ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>      for(ir in 1:J)
>         beta_raw[ir] ~ student_t(df[SDClass[ir]], 0, 1);
> }
>
> Ross Boylan

parameterization, what would a better prior have been?

Bob asked if the results were reasonable; I didn't look at them too
closely, but they didn't look too bad.  The df distributions had a
large tail, which actually may be part of the problem: the scale for
df is highly elastic, with small changes making a big difference at
the bottom but having almost no effect for large values:

df[1] and sigma_beta[1] go together, for example.

n_eff (<50), most were _raw; relatively few of the transformed
versions were as weak.  In particular, there were no transformed beta
parameters in this group (beta=effects of covariates vs alpha effects

Ross

Andrew leaves these tantalizing hints.  Maybe he'll clarify.

...

> It was also interesting that, among the parameters with the very worst
> n_eff (<50), most were _raw; relatively few of the transformed
> versions were as weak.  In particular, there were no transformed beta
> parameters in this group (beta=effects of covariates vs alpha effects
> of cluster).

I don't know what to make of this.  On the one hand, the non-raw ones
are what we care about.  On the other, the _raw ones are what is actually
being sampled by the sampler.

One case where you really don't care about the raw values is when
they aren't properly identified compared to the transformed versions.

> P.S.  Who is Matt?

Matt Hoffman:

   http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~mdhoffma/

He invented NUTS, which is Stan's default sampler.

He also invented stochastic variational inference, which we're
working on building into Stan.

- Bob

n 10/10/13 7:04 PM, Ross Boylan wrote:
> While trying to estimate a model with a truncated poisson distribution I
> got
> Initialization failed after 100 attempts.  Try specifying initial
> values, reducing ranges of constrained values, or reparameterizing the
> model.
>
> I got this for all 3 chains in the production run, though I did not get
> it in my initial trial run with a different seed.
>
> This was with development code c Sep 12 (currently running more recent
> code, but busy with the multinomial).
>
> It didn't seem too much could go wrong, and so I was surprised by the
> difficulties.  Perhaps largish value of the linear parameter are causing
> trouble when exponentiated?  I gave the first parameter a uniform prior
> on [-5, 5], and exp(5) might be too much.

It's 150 --- is that too much?  Is 1/150 too little?

You can try with init=0 and see if that works.

> Several questions or issues:
> 1) Exactly how  does stan generate random initial values?  I can't find
> much about it, though I thought I saw that they were drawn from [0, 2].

The random initial values are drawn uniformly from [-2,2] on
the unconstrained scale.  The transforms are in the transform chapter.

I'll add more to the doc.

> 2) Is there a way to find more precisely what is failing?

You can evaluate the gradients using test_grad=TRUE on the
Stan call.  That'll evaluate the log prob and gradients at
your init values (given by you or randomly initialized or
initialized to 0).

You can print as you go.  What causes it to fail is a -infinity
or NaN value.   You can get those, for instance, if you provide
variables outside of the support of a distribution, or if there
are underflows or overflows in arithmetic.

> 3) Have I made some goof in my model?

Not that I can see.

It looks like your data declaration matches the truncation.

The exp() is the most likely thing to cause overflow/underflow problems.
In general, you should worry if you need exp() of large values.

> 4) I don't relish generating a set of over-dispersed values for my
> parameters on my own.

It's just the parameters:

 > parameters {
 >      vector[J] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
 >      vector[NCLUSTER] alpha_raw; // cluster effects
 >      real<lower=0> sigma;
 >      real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
 > }

That'd be easy to generate in R -- they all have either
cauchy, normal, or uniform distributions.

> The R documentation is a tad opaque; in
> particular I'm not sure what this option for init means:
> "a list of initial parameter values with
>            which to indicate how the initial values of parameters are
>            specified"
> It sounds very meta.

:-)  I think it's more redundant than meta.  The usual thing
to pass in is a function that returns a list of parameter values.
You might be able to pass in a plain old list.

- Bob

On 10/10/13 5:57 PM, Devin Leopold wrote:
> I have been having some trouble implementing a variance structure for a fairly simple linear model of some vegetation
> cover data using rstan. It is possible I am getting something very basic wrong here and I would appreciate any advise or
> guidance.
>
> I have two response variables I would like to model separately (y1 and y2 in the attached data), they are different ways
> of calculating relative dominance of species in plots. I have drastically simplified the model and data to try and
> trouble shoot here, but the basic problem remains the same.

Thanks for simplifying!  It's a huge help for us.

> The data consists of 1573 observations of 15 species in 261
> plots, with not all species occurring in all plots. I started by simply modeling the response variable as a linear
> combination of an intercept, a predictor variable, x, and random effects of species and plot. The problem arises when I
> attempt to include a variance structure, where the modeled mean response variable has a unique variance for each species
> (similar to the varIdent parameter in the nlme package in R). Including this variance structure appears to work fine for
> one of the modeled response variables, but not the other. In the one that does not work I end up with huge Rhat values
> and low neff (2). When I look at the parameter traces for the model that does not work the chains for most parameters
> seem to start off mixing, but then drift to separate values and almost completely stop varying during sampling.

Are some of the scale parameters si... getting very small?

What happens if you try to back off fitting some of the
scale parameters and just set them?

> Interestingly, if I remove the random effect of "plot", but leave in the variance structure (which is based on species)
> the model seems to behave. I can not seem to figure out why the behavior is so different for the two response variables.

Certainly a clue.  Often when models get overparameterized,
they're hard to fit because the parameters aren't well identified.

> The only obvious difference between the two response variables is that the problematic one is much less variable within
> plots (in some plots all species have the same value, leading to zero variation between species in that plot),

Could this cause an identification problem?  Or is there
a hierarchical variance or scale parameter going to zero?

It sounds like the right place to investigate.

You might try fitting the model with simulated data of different shapes.
Sorry to turn this into an investigative modeling problem.
Someone else might have a better idea just from looking at the
model.

? but this

> does not seem to cause a problem when I do not include the variance structure based on species.

This again seems to point to an overparameterization.

It seems like you've diagnosed the interaction causing the problem.
But if there were too many degrees of freedom, you'd expect to see the
posterior wander all over, not get stuck.

Also, you're giving the scale parameters very broad priors if you're not expecting
values near 100.  Ditto the regression parameters, because of the normal(0,1000)
priors.  Tightening those to something more realistic should help inference.

- Bob

messages.subject: Bounding a parameter by another parameter in a hierarchical model.
messages.subject_clean: Bounding a parameter by another parameter in a hierarchical model.
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I’m attempting to estimate a hierarchical double exponential mixture model (two shifted exponetials, actually). The model is fitted to inter-response times of rats, where the inter-response times of each rat are fit to the double-exponential, and the parameters of the double exponential are assumed to be log-normally distributed at the group level.

I’ve gotten the non-hierarchical version of the model to work, however, the bounding of parameters is giving me some trouble in the hierarchical model. One parameter (pW0) can never be smaller than another (pB0).

In the non-hierarchical case, it’s a simple matter of:

real<lower=pB0,upper=positive_infinity()> pW0;

However, in the hierarchical case, pW0 and pB0 are vectors (one value for each rat).  How can I set the bounds so that the lower bound of pW0 for each rat is that rat’s pB0?

For-loops don’t seem to work in the parameter designation area, giving the following error:

EXPECTATION FAILURE LOCATION: file=input; line=16, column=3

  for (r in 1:rat_count) {

  ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

Parser expecting: "}">

 Similarly, the parameter that shifts the distribution of response times, pDelta, should be constrained so that it can never be larger than the smallest response time (min_irt) for each animal. However, I have similar problem deciding how to write the code where each individual minimum response time serves as the upper bounds for each individual’s pDelta.

I suspect there’s a simple trick using vectors that I’m unaware of. If anyone could offer some advice, I’d greatly appreciate it!

I’ve attached the model and R script, along with sample data files.

-Ryan

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] student-t and Matt trick
messages.body_plain:
R
One take on this is that t-distribution errors could be thought of as arising from a mixture model, in which case that mixture distribution can be modeled directly.
It is known that low-df t models can have convergence problems because of multimodality, which in some sense can be thought of as discrete aspects of the mixture model.
A

P.S.  Thanks for interacting on this.  The discussion is helpful to me.

On Oct 11, 2013, at 2:23 AM, Ross Boylan wrote:

> On Thu, 2013-10-10 at 22:02 +0200, Andrew Gelman wrote:
>> I'm not sure the best prior for df, but I assume you'd want to restrict df to be greater than 1 or even to restrict to be greater than 2.  One possibility could be an exponential distribution on (df-1) or (df-2) with scale 5.
>> In the past I've tried parameterizing on 1/df but that doesn't seem quite right either.
>> A
>
> I put the above suggestion with that  of earlier emails, and the results
> are still not very good.  I did apply a sqrt to the variance
> normalization, which seemed right for a scale parameter.  There was a
> floor of 2.01 on the df values.
>
> Running 3 parallel chains of 2000 iterations each, reducing the warmup
> to 500, ended up with a minimum n_eff of 11 (though Q1 of n_eff was >
> 2,000). About 2/3 hour wall time. The substantive estimates I checked
> looked pretty much the same as with the normal model.
>
> I guess in this case, relative simplicity wins.
>
> The parameter with the lowest n_eff (one of the beta) had an odd trace:
> one of the chains showed much higher variability than the others (also
> the worst Rhat at 1.11).  None of the chains looked stuck.  All the
> chains looked very similar during warmup; it was only after that they
> diverged.  The relevant df and scale parameters are very low and very
> high respectively during the periods of high variability of the beta in
> that chain.  However, the other chains also exhibit periods of low
> beta/high scale.
>
> Maybe moving the floor of the df even higher would prevent the extreme
> scale values they produce.  It looks as if the attempt to separate
> sigma_beta into independent parameters for scale and df didn't work; df
> and scale appear more coupled than df and sigma_beta.
>
> Here's the code, if anyone is curious:
> data {
>   int<lower=0> N; // number of partners
>   int<lower=2> K; // number of types of partner race
>       // K is the number of categories in the outcome pEthnic
>   int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates
>   int<lower=0> NSD;  // number of classes of beta for sd
>   int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J];  // beta[j, k] has sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
>   int<lower=1,upper=K> pEthnic[N];  // partner race
>   int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of respondents
>   int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
>   row_vector[J] x[N];  // covariates
> }
> parameters {
>    matrix[J, K] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
>    vector[K] alpha_raw[NCLUSTER]; // cluster effects
>    real<lower=0> sigma;
>    real<lower=0> scale_beta[NSD];
>    vector<lower=0>[NSD] df_raw; // df for t distn minimum value 2.01
> }
> transformed parameters {
>    matrix [J, K] beta;
>    vector[K] alpha[NCLUSTER];
>    vector<lower=0>[NSD] sigma_beta;
>    for (i in 1:NSD)
>       sigma_beta[i] <- scale_beta[i]*sqrt((df_raw[i]+.01)/(df_raw[i]+2.01));
>    for(ir in 1:J)
>       beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
>    for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
>      alpha[i] <- alpha_raw[i]*sigma;
> }
> model {
>    vector[K] beta_x;
>    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>    scale_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
>    df_raw ~ exponential(0.2);
>    for(ir in 1:J)
>       beta_raw[ir] ~ student_t(2.01+df_raw[SDClass[ir]], 0, 1);
>    for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
>      alpha_raw[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
>    for(n in 1:N) {
>      beta_x <- (x[n] * beta)'+alpha[iCluster[n]];
>      pEthnic[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta_x);
>    }
> }
>
> 3 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=500; thin=1;
> post-warmup draws per chain=1500, total post-warmup draws=4500.
>
>              mean se_mean  sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75% 97.5% n_eff Rhat

> # df = df_raw + 2.01

> df_raw[2]      1.7     0.2 2.9  0.0 0.1 0.6 1.9  10.3   242    1
> df_raw[3]      2.6     0.5 4.0  0.0 0.2 0.9 3.1  14.1    78    1
> scale_beta[1]  1.7     0.0 1.1  0.7 1.1 1.4 1.9   4.0   617    1

messages.subject: Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?
messages.subject_clean: Coercing Real to Int for Poisson with Censored Data?
messages.body_plain:
I am working on analyzing data on the number of offspring reared to reproductive age as a function of the number conceived by a given woman, in order to investigate quantity quality tradeoffs in a non-industrial population.

There are three kinds of records:
1) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and complete rearing records (all offspring are either dead or over 18).
2) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and incomplete rearing records (some offspring are alive and under 18).
3) Women who have incomplete conception records (women are alive and under 55 years old) and incomplete rearing records.

The first kind of record is easily handled with a standard Poisson. The second kind of record can be handled by integrating over the censored records as described in the manual, since we know that the outcome is constrained to fall between the observed counts of reared offspring and the total count of conceptions minus offspring who have died.

The third kind of record is more challenging, since we need to impute the number of conceptions (given the location of the woman on the reproductive life course), this can be imputed as a real without much harm (i think) since it is inside the linear model for lambda.

Next what I would like to do is for every imputed value of number of conceptions,X, take floor(X), and use this as the upper limit on the number of possible reared offspring when integrating out the censored records. This will limited the area of the CDF being integrated over to remain under the imputed number of conceptions.

To do this I need floor(X) to be an int, but it can't figure out how to make it so. I also don't know if this is 'shenanigans' given how HMC works.

On 10/11/13 4:02 PM, Cody Ross wrote:
>
>   I am working on analyzing data on the number of offspring reared to reproductive age as a function of the number
> conceived by a given woman, in order to investigate quantity quality tradeoffs in a non-industrial population.
>
> There are three kinds of records:
> 1) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and complete rearing records (all
> offspring are either dead or over 18).
> 2) Women who have complete conception records (women are either dead or >55 years old) and incomplete rearing records
> (some offspring are alive and under 18).
> 3) Women who have incomplete conception records (women are alive and under 55 years old) and incomplete rearing records.
>
> The first kind of record is easily handled with a standard Poisson. The second kind of record can be handled by
> integrating over the censored records as described in the manual, since we know that the outcome is constrained to fall
> between the observed counts of reared offspring and the total count of conceptions minus offspring who have died.

You might be able to use a difference of CDFs here, too,
depending on how simple the model is.  The problem is when
the span gets big, you get a big summation in the direct
marginalization.

> The third kind of record is more challenging, since we need to impute the number of conceptions (given the location of
> the woman on the reproductive life course), this can be imputed as a real without much harm (i think) since it is inside
> the linear model for lambda.
>
> Next what I would like to do is for every imputed value of number of conceptions,X, take floor(X), and use this as the
> upper limit on the number of possible reared offspring when integrating out the censored records. This will limited the
> area of the CDF being integrated over to remain under the imputed number of conceptions.
>
> To do this I need floor(X) to be an int, but it can't figure out how to make it so. I also don't know if this is
> 'shenanigans' given how HMC works.

We've tried to discourage real to int conversions, as they lose the
gradient information in HMC.  floor() is also bad if the value being
floored is a real parameter that needs to be estimated, because the
derivative is 0 everywhere but where the function's discontinuous.
Stan's search then becomes a random walk.

It might work anyway, but you'd need a way to get an int in order to
pass it into Poisson, which requires an int argument.

You could hack it up using int_step and a loop, but that's super ugly.

   convert x to floor(x) as int

   real x;
   int floor_x;
   {
      floor_x <- 0;
      while (!int_step(x - floor_x))
        n <- n + 1;
      v <- n;
   }

But it's probably not a good idea.

Maybe you can code up the density you want using a real-value
in the CDF.  You can use our floor() function for that because
it's fed into a gamma function.  The Poisson's CDF is pretty simple:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poisson_distribution

Maybe somebody else will have a better idea.

Or maybe somebody will motivate the function:

    int round(real);

But we'd have to red flag it everywhere because it's unsafe
in Stan.  (We should probably also issue warnings on uses of
floor() for the same reason.)

- Bob
